extracted.intended_audience: funding agency staff, ERC program designers, science policy researchers, and peer review scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Rubric and practice for assessing frontier research grant applications in ERC-style peer review, with emphasis on tensions between funding high-risk/high-reward ‘ground‑breaking’ projects and panels' conservative tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific excellence (stated single criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: ERC's declared sole evaluation criterion: 'Scientific excellence' applied to ground‑breaking nature, ambition, feasibility, intellectual capacity, creativity, and commitment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied dimensions listed by ERC: 1) ground‑breaking nature of the research idea; 2) ambition of the proposed work; 3) feasibility within the timeframe; 4) intellectual capacity of the PI; 5) creativity of the PI; 6) commitment of the PI. Luukkonen warns that using a single umbrella criterion 'excellence' risks producing conservative outcomes unless countermeasures are explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground‑breaking nature of the research idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether the proposal is genuinely novel and frontier‑pushing ('ground‑breaking').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the stated 'scientific excellence' criterion; in practice panels struggle to operationalize genuine novelty because novelty often lacks supporting methods or data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition of the proposed work
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of the scale, scope, and boldness of the research aims ('ambition').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambition is valued in principle but may be penalized in practice if it reduces clarity/feasibility signals panels look for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility within the timeframe
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether the planned work can realistically be accomplished within the proposal's time and resource constraints ('feasibility').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels heavily weigh feasibility; this often disadvantages high‑risk proposals that are inherently less developed methodologically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual capacity of the PI
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the principal investigator's demonstrated intellectual ability to carry out the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often operationalized via CV, prior publications, and evidence of leadership; used as a proxy for future success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creativity of the PI
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the PI's originality and ability to produce novel ideas or approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the 'excellence' rubric but hard to quantify; panels may prefer demonstrable track record over speculative creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment of the PI
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment of the PI's dedication and availability to carry the project through ('commitment').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice inferred from time allocation, institutional support, and prior sustained research output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track record of past output (operational criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists heavily weight applicants' prior publication and output records despite 'excellence' being the formal criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Luukkonen reports panels use past output as a major de facto selection filter; can disadvantage promising early‑career or unconventional researchers without traditional metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of hypotheses or research questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for proposals that present sharp, well‑formed hypotheses or research questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels favor clear, tightly articulated aims; truly exploratory or open‑ended frontier research with vague questions is often penalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed methodological plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectation that proposals include a concrete, detailed plan of methods and approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when 'ground‑breaking' work may require flexible or novel methods, panels reward detailed Method sections — penalizing open‑ended or exploratory methodologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary data demonstrating viability
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for proposals that present pilot data or other evidence that the approach is viable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels reward preliminary results as risk‑mitigating evidence; absence of such data harms truly novel proposals that, by definition, lack prior results.

rubrics_metrics.name: CV‑based assessment of PI's prior excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of CV items (publications, grants, awards) to infer the PI's excellence and future potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically conflated with 'track record'; can bias selection toward established researchers and conventional career paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal coherence and writing quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of how well the proposal is written and coherently structured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, well‑written proposals are favored; communicative clarity can outweigh conceptual novelty in panel decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty for under‑developed methodologies (anti‑ground‑breaking pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: High‑risk proposals are penalized because they typically have less developed methodologies, and panels favor detailed methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Luukkonen documents this as a systematic barrier to funding genuinely innovative projects; design rubrics must avoid equating detailed method descriptions with scientific value in all cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty for lack of preliminary data (anti‑ground‑breaking pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Truly novel proposals often lack pilot data and are therefore disadvantaged by reviewers who reward preliminary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This incentivizes conservative, incremental research; rubrics should explicitly allow low‑evidence/high‑novelty cases or provide alternative evidence modalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus‑driven lowest‑common‑denominator novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel consensus dynamics push selection toward proposals that all members can endorse, reducing acceptance of bold, divisive ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group decision processes can suppress high‑risk options; rubric design can counteract this by protecting projects that generate disagreement yet score highly on novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer paradigm bias / disadvantage for paradigm‑crossing work
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers' own commitments to existing paradigms disadvantage proposals that cross or challenge disciplinary boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Luukkonen highlights disciplinary bias as a structural conservatism; rubrics should include measures for disciplinary distance and mechanisms to value paradigm‑crossing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounding conservatism in two‑stage review
rubrics_metrics.description: Multi‑stage processes (panel plus external review) can compound conservative selection pressures at each stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each stage may apply conservative filters; consider stage‑specific criteria or safeguards to preserve high‑risk candidates through evaluation phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview stage favors confident communicators over originality
rubrics_metrics.description: At interview/defense stages, confident presentation skills are rewarded, which may advantage communicators rather than the most original thinkers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committees may conflate presentation polish with intellectual merit; rubrics should separate communication skill from conceptual novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow funding where panel disagreement is high (reform implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate rubric element: explicitly permit or require some funding of proposals with high panel disagreement as a proxy for high novelty/risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Luukkonen recommends this as a countermeasure to consensus‑driven conservatism — e.g., set aside funds for controversial/high‑novelty proposals or use alternate decision rules when disagreement is high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight novelty/risk separately from feasibility/track record (reform implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design rubric to score novelty and risk as distinct axes, rather than conflating them under 'excellence' with feasibility/track record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate weighting allows high‑novelty proposals to be recognized even if feasibility signals (methods, preliminary data, track record) are weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lottery among high‑novelty proposals where consensus is impossible (reform implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce randomized selection (lottery) among proposals judged high‑novelty when panels cannot reach consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested as a pragmatic way to break selection deadlocks and reduce conservative bias; must be paired with transparent eligibility rules for the lottery pool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audit funded portfolio for paradigm‑crossing and disciplinary distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor and evaluate the funded portfolio to ensure support for paradigm‑crossing and disciplinary distance from prior work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use portfolio audits to detect and correct conservative tendencies; track measures of disciplinary distance and novelty in funded projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta‑principle: single 'excellence' criterion risks conservatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rubric using 'excellence' as its sole, undifferentiated criterion will tend toward conservatism unless deliberately counteracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Luukkonen's central implication: operationalizing 'excellence' requires explicit subcriteria and safeguards (e.g., separate novelty axis, disagreement‑friendly procedures) to achieve funding of truly high‑risk/high‑reward science.
